root_cause.text: The sched/mmcid code in sched_mm_cid_exit() wrongly assumed per-CPU mm_cid state was always CPU-owned during a mode switch, so mm_drop_cid_on_cpu() operated on a TRANSIT-tagged cid without verifying the ONCPU bit and used that encoded value as a bitmap index.
root_cause.evidence: The commit message states “sched_mm_cid_exit() assumes that the CID is CPU owned because the prior mode was per CPU” and that this led to “clear_bit() with an insanely large bit number because TRANSIT is set (bit 29)”; the patch fixes this by adding `if (cid_on_cpu(pcp->cid))` before converting and dropping the CPU cid in `mm_drop_cid_on_cpu()`.

intent_record.intent_summary: Clarify the sched_mm_cid_exit() comment to better describe CID and TRANSIT-bit handling during mode changes.
intent_record.what: The change updates a comment in sched_mm_cid_exit() by replacing the explanation about the CPU CID still being valid and not having MM_CID_TRANSIT set after a mode change with new wording stating that the task already has the CID unset and has already handled any possibly set TRANSIT bit, and that the CID should be dropped only if it is owned by the CPU.
intent_record.how: This does not alter runtime behavior because no executable code is changed; it clarifies the conditions and rationale for the existing mm_drop_cid_on_cpu() call during a mode change.

intent_record.intent_summary: Guard CID release so mm_drop_cid_on_cpu() only drops CIDs that are actually marked on-CPU.
intent_record.what: The function mm_drop_cid_on_cpu() was changed to wrap the existing conversion and drop logic in an if (cid_on_cpu(pcp->cid)) conditional, so pcp->cid is converted with cpu_cid_to_cid() and passed to mm_drop_cid() only when the ONCPU bit is set.
intent_record.how: At runtime, this prevents mm_drop_cid_on_cpu() from dropping a CID unless the per-CPU CID is actually marked as on-CPU, avoiding unnecessary or incorrect CID conversion and release when pcp->cid is not in the ONCPU state.

grouping_result.intent: Clarify the sched_mm_cid_exit() comment to better describe CID and TRANSIT-bit handling during mode changes.
Guard CID release so mm_drop_cid_on_cpu() only drops CIDs that are actually marked on-CPU.

relevance_review.reason: The change directly concerns sched_mm_cid_exit() and specifically clarifies CID/TRANSIT-bit handling during mode changes, which is the exact area and mechanism involved in the root cause.

The change directly addresses the root cause by adding an ONCPU-state check before dropping a CID, preventing mm_drop_cid_on_cpu() from acting on a TRANSIT-tagged encoded value as if it were a valid on-CPU bitmap index.

candidates.rationale: This directly uses pcp->cid as the bitmap index after only applying cpu_cid_to_cid(), without verifying that the CID is actually marked ONCPU. If pcp->cid is TRANSIT-tagged during the mode switch, this can pass an invalid encoded value into mm_drop_cid().

This statement assumes the per-CPU CID can be blindly converted by clearing the ONCPU bit, but it does not check whether the ONCPU bit was present. With a TRANSIT-tagged CID, the encoded state remains unsuitable for release and leads to misuse as a CID index.

This call embodies the faulty assumption in sched_mm_cid_exit() that the local per-CPU CID is always CPU-owned and safe to drop during a mode switch. It invokes the drop helper on state that may instead be TRANSIT-tagged.

vuln_statements.explanation: This is the unsafe release operation that uses pcp->cid as the CID/bitmap index without first verifying that the per-CPU state is actually marked ONCPU. When pcp->cid is TRANSIT-tagged during the mode switch, this statement causes the encoded value to be consumed as a CID index, matching the root cause.

This conversion clears the ONCPU encoding assumption without checking that the ONCPU bit was ever set. If the state is TRANSIT-tagged instead of CPU-owned, this produces an invalid value that is then passed to the drop path, enabling the misuse described in the root cause.

This call site in sched_mm_cid_exit() reflects the incorrect assumption that the local per-CPU mm_cid state is always CPU-owned during the mode switch. It invokes the helper on state that may be TRANSIT-tagged, triggering the faulty conversion and drop sequence.

The root cause involves operating on a TRANSIT-tagged per-CPU cid without verifying ONCPU and then using that encoded value as a bitmap index. In this version, that complex tagged-state machinery is gone. The diff removes the prior stateful per-cpu handling (`mm_cid_put_lazy`, `mm_cid_pcpu_unset`, lazy/valid/unset transitions, cmpxchg-based state machine) and replaces it with simple plain integer CIDs. The root cause describes a bug where exit/drop logic could operate on a TRANSIT-tagged per-CPU cid without checking an ONCPU bit, and then use that encoded value as a bitmap index. In this commit, that complex state machine is gone from the shown code: there are no TRANSIT/ONCPU-tagged states, no encoded per-CPU cid state transitions, and no mm_drop_cid_on_cpu()-style logic at all. Since the vulnerable construct depends on TRANSIT-tagged values being interpreted as bitmap indices without verifying ownership/ONCPU state, and this code no longer contains that representation or logic, the vulnerable construct is absent.     sched/mmcid: Drop per CPU CID immediately when switching to per task mode
    
    When a exiting task initiates the switch from per CPU back to per task

bic_trace_step.reason: The snippet is sufficient because it shows the exact mode-switch handling inside `sched_mm_cid_exit()` that the root cause discusses. In this commit, the old vulnerable behavior is gone: the deleted lines were `/* Mode change required. Transfer currents CID */` followed by `mm_cid_transit_to_task(current, this_cpu_ptr(mm->mm_cid.pcpu));`, which would reassign/mark the per-CPU CID as in-transit for the exiting task. That is replaced with `mm_drop_cid_on_cpu(mm, this_cpu_ptr(mm->mm_cid.pcpu));` and an explanatory comment: `The task has the CID unset already.
